Conditional on a Special Issuance, and only as a single agent. The FAA lists it under "CONDITIONALLY Acceptable Antidepressant Medications with SI", "Used as a single agent, if otherwise qualified." It names the drug "citalopram (Celexa)".

On Item 47 the FAA states "The AME may not issue" and that "The Authorization decision is made on a case-by-case basis." Its criteria start with the diagnosis: "The applicant has one of the following diagnoses: Major depressive disorder (mild to moderate) either single episode or recurrent episode", "Dysthymic disorder", "Adjustment disorder with depressed mood", or "Any non-depression related condition for which the SSRI is used". Then "For a minimum of 3 continuous months prior, the applicant has been clinically stable as well as on a stable dose of medication without any aeromedically significant side effects and/or an increase in symptoms"; the medication must be one of the conditionally acceptable ones, "single use only; not in combination"; and the applicant "must be further evaluated by a Human Intervention Motivation Study (HIMS) AME." The FAA's answer depends on whether you have a diagnosis of diabetes, not on the brand.

With a diagnosis of diabetes the diabetes pathway applies even when the prescription is for weight loss: the FAA writes "If used for DIABETES, see www.faa.gov/go/diabetic", and there the AME defers at initial certification.

With no diagnosis of diabetes, taken for weight loss, the FAA lists semaglutide under "ACCEPTABLE Weight Loss Medications", "When certification criteria are met", with a CACI worksheet the AME can work from.

There is a third path the FAA keeps separate: it says "See either the Prediabetes or Weight Loss Management disposition tables", and its worksheet notes "If A1c is in the prediabetic range (5.7 to 6.4%)" to "see the Pre-Diabetes page".

Its Acceptable Combinations chart places semaglutide in Group D (GLP1 mimetics) and says "Only ONE Medication allowed from each group (A–G)". "When certification criteria are met", the FAA lists Wegovy under "ACCEPTABLE Weight Loss Medications".

It names it "semaglutide (Wegovy)".

Its criteria: "A1C must be 6.4 or less with no diagnosis of diabetes", "No history of hypoglycemia requiring intervention", and "One (1) week after starting for weight loss." It also requires "48-hour observation with each dose increase, medication, or formulation change." Its Weight Loss Management disposition table is ISSUE on ONE non-insulin diabetic medication component, and on "TWO (2) or more" it is DEFER, "Submit the information to the FAA for a possible Special Issuance".

Even the ISSUE is not automatic: it "requires a current, detailed Clinical Progress Note from the treating physician and Hemoglobin A1c lab performed no more than 90 days before the AME exam", or a "Weight Loss Management Status Report".

Its CACI worksheet takes "ONLY ONE of the medications listed", says "If the applicant has EVER had an A1C OF 6.5% OR GREATER, DO NOT USE THIS CACI." and that "Diabetes in remission (diet-controlled), diabetes treated with medication (including insulin), or diabetes insipidus DO NOT qualify for this CACI." faaStatusDescription:
Conditional on a Special Issuance, and only as a single agent. The FAA lists it under "CONDITIONALLY Acceptable Antidepressant Medications with SI", "Used as a single agent, if otherwise qualified." It names the drug "sertraline (Zoloft)".

On Item 47 the FAA states "The AME may not issue" and that "The Authorization decision is made on a case-by-case basis." Its criteria start with the diagnosis: "The applicant has one of the following diagnoses: Major depressive disorder (mild to moderate) either single episode or recurrent episode", "Dysthymic disorder", "Adjustment disorder with depressed mood", or "Any non-depression related condition for which the SSRI is used". Then "For a minimum of 3 continuous months prior, the applicant has been clinically stable as well as on a stable dose of medication without any aeromedically significant side effects and/or an increase in symptoms"; the medication must be one of the conditionally acceptable ones, "single use only; not in combination"; and the applicant "must be further evaluated by a Human Intervention Motivation Study (HIMS) AME." It also requires that "The applicant DOES NOT have symptoms or history of" psychosis, suicidal ideation, electro convulsive therapy, treatment with multiple SSRIs concurrently, or multi-agent drug protocol use.

Stopping the medication before an exam is its own path, not a shortcut. Where an airman "opts to discontinue use of the SSRI", the FAA says "the Examiner must notate in Block 60, Comments on History and Findings, on FAA Form 8500-8 and defer issuance", and to reapply for regular issuance the applicant "must be off the medication for a minimum of 60 days with a favorable report from the treating physician indicating stable mood and no aeromedically significant side effects".

The FAA renamed this pathway the Antidepressant Protocol; older references to an SSRI protocol are "considered encompassed in the Antidepressant Protocol".

Confirm against the current AME Guide and a qualified AME.

Conditional on a Special Issuance, and only as a single agent. The FAA lists it under "CONDITIONALLY Acceptable Antidepressant Medications with SI", "Used as a single agent, if otherwise qualified." It names the drug "venlafaxine (Effexor)".

On Item 47 the FAA states "The AME may not issue" and that "The Authorization decision is made on a case-by-case basis." Its criteria start with the diagnosis: "The applicant has one of the following diagnoses: Major depressive disorder (mild to moderate) either single episode or recurrent episode", "Dysthymic disorder", "Adjustment disorder with depressed mood", or "Any non-depression related condition for which the SSRI is used". Then "For a minimum of 3 continuous months prior, the applicant has been clinically stable as well as on a stable dose of medication without any aeromedically significant side effects and/or an increase in symptoms"; the medication must be one of the conditionally acceptable ones, "single use only; not in combination"; and the applicant "must be further evaluated by a Human Intervention Motivation Study (HIMS) AME." It also requires that "The applicant DOES NOT have symptoms or history of" psychosis, suicidal ideation, electro convulsive therapy, treatment with multiple SSRIs concurrently, or multi-agent drug protocol use.

Stopping the medication before an exam is its own path, not a shortcut. Where an airman "opts to discontinue use of the SSRI", the FAA says "the Examiner must notate in Block 60, Comments on History and Findings, on FAA Form 8500-8 and defer issuance", and to reapply for regular issuance the applicant "must be off the medication for a minimum of 60 days with a favorable report from the treating physician indicating stable mood and no aeromedically significant side effects".

The FAA renamed this pathway the Antidepressant Protocol; older references to an SSRI protocol are "considered encompassed in the Antidepressant Protocol".

Confirm against the current AME Guide and a qualified AME.
